title: Convert List to Set — what happens to duplicates
shortTitle: Convert List to Set — what happens to duplicates

s1_definition.profdef: Converting a List to a Set removes duplicates, and which Set you choose decides the resulting order. `new HashSet<>(list)` drops duplicates and loses order; `new LinkedHashSet<>(list)` drops duplicates and keeps insertion order; `new TreeSet<>(list)` drops duplicates and sorts the result. The stream form `list.stream().collect(Collectors.toSet())` produces an unordered HashSet.
s1_definition.analogy: You pour a stack of account cards (some duplicated) into a de-duplicating tray. A HashSet tray keeps one of each but shuffles them; a LinkedHashSet tray keeps one of each in arrival order; a TreeSet tray keeps one of each sorted alphabetically.
s1_definition.oneliner: List to Set removes duplicates; HashSet loses order, LinkedHashSet keeps insertion order, TreeSet sorts.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Converting a List to a Set removes duplicates, and which Set you choose decides the resulting order. `new HashSet<>(list)` drops duplicates and loses order; `new LinkedHashSet<>(list)` drops duplicates and keeps insertion order; `new TreeSet<>(list)` drops duplicates and sorts the result. The stream form `list.stream().collect(Collectors.toSet())` produces an unordered HashSet.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** You pour a stack of account cards (some duplicated) into a de-duplicating tray. A HashSet tray keeps one of each but shuffles them; a LinkedHashSet tray keeps one of each in arrival order; a TreeSet tray keeps one of each sorted alphabetically.

**One line to remember:** List to Set removes duplicates; HashSet loses order, LinkedHashSet keeps insertion order, TreeSet sorts.

sections.s2_technical:
The duplicate removal uses `equals` and `hashCode`, so the first occurrence is kept and later equal elements are discarded.

```java
import java.util.*;

List<String> names = new ArrayList<>(List.of("Rajesh", "Priya", "Rajesh", "Amit"));
Set<String> unordered = new HashSet<>(names);        // order unpredictable
Set<String> ordered   = new LinkedHashSet<>(names);  // [Rajesh, Priya, Amit]
Set<String> sorted    = new TreeSet<>(names);         // [Amit, Priya, Rajesh]
```

The senior point: pick the Set type by the ordering guarantee you need downstream, because silently losing order in a report or statement is a common and avoidable bug.
sections.s3_banking: At the National Bank of India this came up directly when handling converting a List to a Set. Rajesh holds savings account SAV2001 with a balance of 1,000,000 rupees and Priya holds current account CUR3001 with 250,000 rupees, and the team needed the collection behaviour to be exactly correct so balances and account lists were never wrong. sections.s6_takeaway:
Converting a List to a Set removes duplicates using equals and hashCode, and the Set implementation you choose determines the ordering of the result. A HashSet loses order, a LinkedHashSet preserves insertion order, and a TreeSet returns the elements sorted.

In the National Bank reporting pipeline I frequently deduplicated lists of account identifiers, and I always chose the Set type deliberately. When the audit output needed to match the original arrival order of accounts such as Rajesh's and Priya's I used a LinkedHashSet, and when it needed to be sorted I used a TreeSet, so the deduplication never accidentally scrambled a customer-facing statement.

In an interview I would stress that I always use BigDecimal for money, keep map keys immutable, and pick the collection whose ordering and complexity match the banking access pattern, because in a system that moves real money, choosing the wrong data structure is not a style issue, it is a correctness and reliability issue.
